title: The Civic Bestiary
description: A field guide to the characters of the body politic: portmanteaus for performative patriotism, bad-faith debate, hypocrisy, and algorithmic radicalization - plus the documented fallacies they commit.
preface: This is a bestiary, not a dictionary. The characters in it are real, common, and close by - the flag hoodie in the school-board queue, the centrist with one newsletter, the commentator monetizing your uncle's anger. Each species is named the way a naturalist would name it: by the trait that makes it unmistakable, and by the psy-loop it runs.

Two rules keep the guide from collapsing into a list of insults. The species is a pattern, not a person - a costume that wears people, not a kind of human, and one you can catch yourself in. And every entry describes a mechanism you could point at in a transcript, a rally, or a comment thread, so the name stays a tool for recognition rather than a way to end an argument.

The coinages are portmanteaus on purpose: legible on first contact, slightly ridiculous on second thought. Some of these characters are trolls in the old sense, things that live under bridges and demand a toll; some are trolls in the newer one. Both are field-observed here. That is roughly the right posture for the subject.

The fallacies work the other way round. They are not coinages and are not ours: they are documented errors in reasoning, named by logicians and studied by psychologists, and every one of them links to its source. Each chapter ends with the documented errors its own characters commit, so the joke arrives with its receipt attached. The definitions here are written in this guide's voice, but nothing in them is invented - if a claim about a fallacy cannot be traced to the literature, it does not go in the record. The errors that turn up in several chapters at once get a chapter of their own, because an error that belongs to everyone is one nobody flinches at any more: that is chapter V, and it is the chapter about the room rather than the people in it. The coinages are the joke; the fallacies are the part you can cite.

chapters.title: Normalization, Numbness & the Noise Floor
chapters.note: Every other chapter points at a character and the errors they commit. This one points at the room: the species who keep it exactly as it is, and the machinery that does the keeping - the soft launch that makes a change official, the clause that exempts what came before, the conference where the consensus is catered, the fatigue that ends the argument by exhausting it. Its fallacies are the ones that turn up in several chapters at once, because an error everyone commits is one nobody flinches at any more. Normalization is what a body politic does with the unacceptable once the flinching stops.

chapters.title: The Keystones
chapters.note: Every character in chapters I to IV has a counterpart with a job title: the clerk who keeps the record, the auditor who reads the books, the poll worker who counts in public. These are the species whose absence is the pathology - and the procedures they actually run.
